content.title: NASA says Artemis II launch is still on target; explains moon base
content.text: WASHINGTON, D.C. — NASA officials say the upcoming Artemis II launch to send four astronauts around the moon from Kennedy Space Center is on track for next week after a helium flow issue caused a delay. What You Need To Know NASA officials explained the moon base and the phases of development The Artemis IV mission will send astronauts to the lunar surface Get more space coverage here ▶ RELATED coverage: NASA repairs helium flow issue that caused Artemis II rollback NASA: Artemis III will not land on the moon NASA to roll back its Artemis II moon rocket for repairs NASA to rollback Artemis moon rocket due to helium flow issue; March launch canceled NASA sets March 6 as earliest moon mission opportunity after successful practice NASA to conduct second wet dress rehearsal of Artemis II NASA to review Artemis II test data as it eyes March launch NASA says it detected leak on Artemis II moon rocket during testing Looking back at Artemis I as NASA makes final preps for Artemis II mission 'Rare arctic outbreak' causes NASA to delay Artemis II fueling test NASA rolls out SLS rocket for Artemis II moon mission And NASA leaders outlined the agency’s plans for a future moon base. Leaders in the space industry gathered in DC on Tuesday to hear NASA’s future plans for lunar exploration and eventually a moon base. “The moon base will not appear overnight. We will invest approximately $20 billion over the next seven years and build it through dozens of missions, working together with commercial and international partners towards a deliberate and achievable plan,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. Artemis II will send a crew of astronauts on a flyby mission to the moon, which is no later than Wednesday, April 1. Isaacman says the Artemis IV mission will send astronauts to the lunar surface and that is targeted for early 2028; then comes Artemis V. “Artemis V is targeted later in 2028 to further accelerate towards establishing the lunar base, said Lori Glaze, acting associate administrator of NASA’s Exploration Systems Development Mission Directorate. Isaacman explained what the development of the moon base would look like. NASA leaders say they are pivoting from its Gateway Program architecture, an orbiting lunar outpost, to instead focus on the lunar surface, hoping to have a “semi-permanent crew presence” starting in 2032. The moon base will have drones, rovers and habitats. “Definitely see a bunch of infrastructure for power, both potentially nuclear, which is maybe shielded to a bunch of solar array towers that are either directly connected to the habitation modules or perhaps on the side at different locations, providing power to some of the assets that are moving around, pressurized rovers, advance LTVs and then different landing sites for human landings, cargo landings,” said NASA Moon Base Program Executive Carlos Garcia-Galan. Florida Republican Congressman Mike Haridopolos, whose district houses Kennedy Space Center, says it’s a “boom for Florida.” “As I like to say, the Space Coast is literally taking off with so many jobs for not only the people there now, but our future, as we're investing in high schools and colleges to make sure that they have the skills to make us the dominant space nation in the world,” he told Spectrum News.
